## Welcome to MATE 374

MATE 374 is a third-year course in computational methods for materials engineering. The course is not only about obtaining an answer from Python or from a simulation package. It is about deciding what should be calculated, choosing a suitable method, and gathering enough evidence to decide whether the answer is useful.

Materials engineers use the word *modeling* for several related activities. We will distinguish three layers.

### Mathematical modeling

A mathematical model turns a physical question into variables, assumptions, and governing relations. It might describe diffusion using a conservation law, phase equilibrium using free energy, or thermal expansion using a constitutive relation. The model is an abstraction: it keeps the features needed for a particular question and leaves others out.

### Numerical modeling and numerical methods

Many mathematical models cannot be solved exactly in the form we need. A numerical method replaces the exact problem with a finite calculation that a computer can carry out. Examples include replacing an infinite series with $N$ terms, locating a root by repeatedly shrinking an interval, or representing a continuous field on a finite grid.

### Computational materials simulation

A materials simulation combines a physical model, numerical methods, material data, and software to study a system at a chosen length and time scale. Density-functional theory, molecular dynamics, Monte Carlo methods, phase-field models, and finite-element models are examples of different model families. They do not answer the same questions, and none of them removes the need for engineering judgement.

These layers form the main thread of the course:

$$
\text{materials question}
\rightarrow
\text{mathematical model}
\rightarrow
\text{numerical representation}
\rightarrow
\text{computation}
\rightarrow
\text{verification and interpretation}.
$$

## What this course emphasizes

Scientific software has changed quickly. Numerical routines once written directly in FORTRAN or C are now available through mature libraries such as NumPy and SciPy. Browser-based Python makes small computational experiments available without a complicated installation. Code-completion tools can also reduce the effort needed to produce a first implementation.

Those changes make numerical judgement more important, not less. By the end of the course, the central skills are to:

- **formulate** a materials question as a mathematical problem;
- **select** a numerical method that fits the problem and the required accuracy;
- **analyze** assumptions, parameters, scales, and sources of error;
- **verify** a result using evidence such as units, residuals, limiting cases, refinement, or conservation;
- **interpret and criticize** the result as a materials engineer;
- **document** enough of the calculation that another person can reproduce it.

Python is the main language used to make these ideas concrete, but this is not a Python syntax course. You will normally begin from a supplied function or notebook and change the part that represents the mathematical idea.

::: {.callout-important}
## A course principle

A program can evaluate almost any equation we can state precisely. That does not mean every equation is a good model, every implementation is correct, or every output deserves trust.
:::

## How to use the course materials

The course website is the main reading and reference source. Each lecture page is designed to work in two ways:

- **before or after class:** read it as a short chapter, with the main definitions, equations, and reasoning in one place;
- **during class:** use the same page for predictions, discussion questions, and links to interactive work.

We will use three recurring tools.

**Wooclap** supports short polls and anonymous class diagnostics. These questions are usually for discussion rather than grades.

**marimo** provides reactive Python notebooks. Many small notebooks run directly in the browser, and a static explanation will be provided when an interactive activity is essential.

**Molab** provides a fuller cloud Python environment for activities that need packages or computing resources that are not practical in a browser-only notebook.

The tool is never the learning objective by itself. A notebook should help us expose a model, compare methods, test a limit, or diagnose a result.

## Course organization

The course is organized into themed units rather than isolated chapters on algorithms.

| Theme | Typical questions | Main computational ideas |
|---|---|---|
| Orientation and numerical thinking | Can we trust this calculation? | approximation, convergence, finite precision, performance |
| Finding special points | Where is an equilibrium, root, or minimum? | bisection, fixed-point iteration, secant and Newton methods, optimization |
| Functions and data | What can values or measurements tell us? | differentiation, integration, interpolation, regression |
| Larger coupled systems | How do many variables interact? | vectors, matrices, linear and nonlinear systems |
| Evolution in time | How does a material state change? | ordinary differential equations, timestep error, stability |
| Evolution in space and time | How do heat, mass, or structure move through a material? | conservation laws, grids, boundary conditions, partial differential equations |
| Simulation across scales | Which description fits the materials question? | continuum, phase field, Monte Carlo, molecular dynamics, electronic structure |

The exact allocation of later lectures may change as the schedule and project are finalized. The underlying progression will remain: formulate, compute, check, and interpret.

## Texts and other resources

The course notes are the main reference. The following sources provide useful alternative explanations and practice:

- Jaan Kiusalaas, [*Numerical Methods in Engineering with Python 3*](https://ualberta.primo.exlibrisgroup.com/view/action/uresolver.do?operation=resolveService&package_service_id=19059219040009116&institutionId=9116&customerId=9115&VE=true).
- Eric Sullivan, [*Numerical Methods: An Inquiry-Based Approach with Python*](https://numericalmethodssullivan.github.io/index.html).
- J. Mmbaga, R. Hayes, K. Nandakumar, and M. Flynn, *Computational Methods for Engineers: Modeling, Algorithms and Analysis*.
- William D. Callister Jr. and David G. Rethwisch, *Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction*, for materials background and example systems.

Use the [course syllabus](../syllabus/index.qmd) for the official resource and support information.

## Before Lecture 1

You do not need to install Python for the first class. Bring a device that can open the course website if possible. If device access is a problem, tell the teaching team so that we can arrange a paired or static route.

If Python feels rusty, work through [Seminar S01 · A crash course in Python for numerical work](../seminars/S01-python-numerics/index.qmd). Keep the Python, NumPy, and SciPy documentation open; the seminar is practice, not a prerequisite test.

The first lecture begins with a more important question than “Can the code run?”:

> **What evidence would make a computational result believable?**
